name: Topology
title: Topology intuition
intro: Topology studies shapes up to continuous deformation — stretching and bending without tearing or gluing. These lessons build intuition for open and closed sets, continuity, homeomorphisms, connectedness and compactness, with examples on the real line and the circle. The tone is conceptual: enough precision to be honest, without a full axiomatic course.

lessons.title: Open and closed sets
lessons.summary: Neighbourhoods on the line; interiors, boundaries and complements.

sections.p: On the real line R, an open interval (a,b) does not include its endpoints. A set U ⊆ R is open if every point of U has some open interval around it still inside U. Open sets are unions of open intervals.

A set is closed if its complement is open. Closed intervals [a,b] include endpoints. Finite sets of points are closed in R. Being closed is not the opposite of “not open”: [0,1) is neither open nor closed in R.
The boundary of [0,1] is {0,1}. Interior points have a whole interval of neighbours inside the set; boundary points do not.

sections.p: In R (usual topology), ∅ and R are both open and closed (“clopen”). That is allowed by the definitions.

lessons.title: Continuity
lessons.summary: No jumps: ε–δ idea and preimages of open sets.

sections.p: A function f: R → R is continuous at a if values f(x) stay close to f(a) whenever x is close to a. Formally: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 so that |x−a| < δ implies |f(x)−f(a)| < ε.
Polynomials, sin, cos, exp and rational functions on their domains (where the denominator ≠ 0) are continuous. A step function with a jump is discontinuous at the jump.
f is continuous (everywhere) iff for every open U in the codomain, the preimage f⁻¹(U) is open in the domain. This definition extends cleanly beyond R.
Composition of continuous maps is continuous. Limits and continuity match when the limit equals the function value.

lessons.title: Homeomorphism idea
lessons.summary: Continuous bijections with continuous inverse — “same shape” topologically.

sections.p: A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection f: X → Y whose inverse is also continuous. If one exists, X and Y are homeomorphic: topologically the same for the purposes of continuous deformation.
You may stretch, bend and reshape, but not cut, tear or glue distant points together. A coffee cup and a doughnut (solid torus) are the classic cartoon — one hole each.

(0,1) is homeomorphic to R (e.g. via tan stretched, or x ↦ (2x−1)/(x(x−1)) variants). [0,1] is not homeomorphic to (0,1): endpoints behave differently (removing an endpoint from [0,1] can leave a connected set; removing a point from (0,1) always splits it).
sections.code:
(0,1) ~ R  (homeomorphic)
[0,1] not ~ (0,1)
Circle S¹ not ~ R

sections.p: Properties preserved by homeomorphism are topological invariants: connectedness, compactness, “number of pieces,” presence of a hole (informally). If an invariant differs, spaces are not homeomorphic.

lessons.title: Connectedness
lessons.summary: One piece versus many; intervals on R.

sections.p: A space is connected if it is not the union of two disjoint nonempty open (in the subspace) sets that cover it — informally, it comes in one piece. On R, the connected subsets are exactly the intervals (including rays, points, R itself).
[0,1] connected; (0,1)∪(2,3) disconnected. The circle is connected. Q (rationals) as a subspace of R is totally disconnected in a strong sense: between any two rationals sits an irrational cut.
Continuous image of a connected set is connected. Intermediate Value Theorem is the special case for f: [a,b] → R: the image is an interval, so every intermediate value is hit.
sections.code:

sections.p: Stronger notion: any two points joined by a continuous path. Open disks in R² are path-connected. Path-connected ⇒ connected; converse can fail in exotic spaces, but for open sets in Rⁿ they agree.

lessons.title: Compactness intuition
lessons.summary: Closed and bounded in Rⁿ; open covers and finite subcovers.

sections.p: Compactness is a finiteness property for infinite spaces. In Rⁿ with the usual metric, Heine–Borel says: a set is compact iff it is closed and bounded. So [0,1] is compact; (0,1) is not (not closed); Z is not (not bounded).

A collection of open sets covers K if their union contains K. K is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. Intuition: infinitely many opens are never all needed; finitely many always suffice.
Cover (0,1) by (1/(n+1), 1−1/(n+1)) for n = 1,2,… — or simpler: unions of (1/n, 1). No finite subcollection reaches down to 0’s neighbourhood inside (0,1).
sections.code:
Compact in R: [0,1], finite sets, empty set
Not compact: (0,1), R, [0,∞), Q∩[0,1]

sections.p: Continuous image of a compact set is compact. Continuous f: [a,b] → R attains max and min (Extreme Value Theorem). Compact + Hausdorff ⇒ closed.

lessons.title: The circle
lessons.summary: S¹ as a compact connected space; loops and cutting points.

sections.p: The circle S¹ = {(x,y): x² + y² = 1} (or R/Z, angles mod 2π) is the simplest space with a hole. It is compact, connected and path-connected.
Remove one point from S¹: what remains is homeomorphic to an open interval — still connected. Remove one point from R: two rays, disconnected. So S¹ ≇ R.

A loop on the circle can wind around the hole n times (integer winding number). You cannot continuously shrink a loop that winds once to a point while staying on the circle — informal hint of fundamental group π₁(S¹) ≅ Z.
Continuous f: S¹ → R must attain max/min and cannot be bijective onto R (compact image in R is closed and bounded). Continuous f: S¹ → S¹ can be classified up to homotopy by degree (winding).

lessons.title: More examples on R
lessons.summary: Subspaces, relative topology and quick classification drills.

sections.p: A subset A ⊆ R inherits a subspace topology: opens in A are intersections of opens in R with A. So (0,1] is open as a subset of (0,1]? — actually (0,1] is open in itself as a whole space, but as a subset of R it is neither open nor closed. Context matters.
In A = [0,1], the set [0,1/2) is open in A (relative to A) because it is (−1/2, 1/2) ∩ A, even though it is not open in R.
sections.code:
In R: [0,½) neither open nor closed
In [0,1]: [0,½) is relatively open

sections.h: Quick invariants on subsets of R
sections.p: Ask: connected? (interval?) compact? (closed and bounded?) homeomorphic to which model interval? Endpoints and whether the set is open/closed in R are the usual clues.

Topology tracks qualitative shape: pieces, holes, boundaries and finiteness of covers — not exact distances. Once those words feel natural on R and S¹, the same vocabulary applies to surfaces, knots and data-shape ideas later.
